To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) in children in Northeast Brazil, biomarkers of enteric barrier integrity and inflammation were associated with stunting and with subsequent growth; 2) these biomarkers can be assessed non-invasively and may help elucidate how enteropathy and inflammation contribute to growth and development in children in resource poor settings; and 3) the findings have implications for the design, implementation and evaluation of interventions for children in resource poor countries.
we have developed a set of non-invasive fecal, urinary, and plasma biomarkers that can be used in children living in resource-limited settings in Brazil, India and Bangladesh.

the gut is a key target for interventions in children living in poverty, and that we need to understand the complex interactions of intestinal barrier disruption with inflammation and LPS translocation in order to design effective interventions to prevent or treat enteropathy.
